NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
What is being proposed: A dual-pressure-vessel architecture with an internal electrolyte reservoir that maintains electrolyte saturation through capillary action and vapor pressure equilibrium. Standard practice uses a single sealed vessel with fixed electrolyte volume, relying on seal integrity alone to prevent electrolyte loss. The adjacent-technique clearance is the use of external humidification systems in some industrial supercapacitors, which is different because our approach is fully sealed, passive, and integrated within the module footprint. The intervention attacks the failure by creating a closed-loop electrolyte management system where any evaporated electrolyte is automatically replenished from the reservoir, maintaining ion transport pathways even at elevated temperatures.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the Clausius-Clapeyron equation for vapor pressure: ln(P2/P1) = (ΔHvap/R)(1/T1 - 1/T2). At 65°C (338K) versus 25°C (298K), with ΔHvap ≈ 40 kJ/mol for typical organic electrolytes, vapor pressure increases by approximately 10×. Our reservoir creates a saturated vapor space, reducing net evaporation rate by establishing equilibrium. The capillary wick (pore size < 10 μm) provides capillary pressure of ΔP = 2γcosθ/r ≈ 20 kPa (for γ=0.03 N/m, θ=0°, r=3μm), sufficient to draw liquid against gravity while allowing vapor transport. This maintains electrolyte contact with electrodes, keeping ESR increase below 10% over 10 years.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Components: 1) Hermetically sealed stainless steel inner vessel (current collector + electrode assembly), 2) Polycarbonate outer pressure vessel with welded seams, 3) Sintered metal wick (316L stainless steel, porosity 40%, pore size 5 μm) connecting reservoir to electrodes, 4) Porous ceramic electrolyte reservoir (alumina, 30% porosity) filled with excess electrolyte (15% more than standard design), 5) Viton O-ring seals between vessels (standard automotive-grade). Materials: Standard electrolyte (TEABF4 in acetonitrile), current collectors (aluminum foil), electrodes (activated carbon). Installation: Weld outer vessel around inner assembly, fill reservoir under vacuum, seal with laser welding. No exotic components required.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Installability: Comparable to standard module assembly (welding is standard process)
- Operability: Identical electrical interface; no operational changes needed
- Maintenance: Zero additional maintenance (passive system)
- Cost: ~15% higher material cost due to dual-vessel and wick, offset by 30% longer life expectancy
- Weight: <3% increase (stainless steel components offset by reduced electrolyte volume)
- Thermal performance: Better than standard (reservoir acts as thermal buffer)
- Constraint compliance: Adds <1 mm height (0.8 mm typical), maintains capacitance loss <10%

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: 10 identical modules, 5 with intervention and 5 without, aged at 85°C/2.7V (accelerated testing) and 65°C/2.7V (operational condition). Measure ESR and capacitance weekly for 1000 hours (85°C) and 3000 hours (65°C). Instruments: LCR meter (ESR/capacitance), thermocouples, gravimetric balance. Pass/fail: Intervention modules must maintain ESR increase <20% and capacitance loss <15% at 85°C after 1000 hours (equivalent to >10 years at 65°C). Kill criterion: If any intervention module exceeds these thresholds, the concept is falsified. Additional validation: Post-mortem analysis of electrolyte distribution in wick and reservoir after testing to confirm capillary action function.
